title: Sum of distances from every node
prompt: Write sumOfDistances(n int, edges [][]int) []int for an undirected tree on nodes 0..n-1 given by n-1 edges. Entry i is the sum of the distances from node i to every other node; a single node gives [0]. It must be O(n) overall: the tests use a 200000-node path and a 200000-node random tree, where running a BFS from each node is O(n^2) and takes minutes.
explanation: This is the rerooting pattern, and it is two linear passes rather than one. Root the tree anywhere. The first pass, processed leaves-upward, computes size[v] (nodes in v's subtree) and down[v] (sum of distances from v to its own subtree), using down[u] += down[v] + size[v]: every node under v is one edge further from u than from v. That only answers the question for the root. The second pass, processed root-downward, moves the answer across one edge at a time: stepping from parent u to child v, the size[v] nodes inside v's subtree each get one step closer and the other n - size[v] nodes each get one step further, so ans[v] = ans[u] + n - 2*size[v]. Both passes are O(n) and the whole thing is O(n) time, O(n) space. The implementation detail worth keeping is the traversal order: a BFS order computed once can be walked backwards for the upward pass and forwards for the downward pass, which avoids recursion depth 200000 on the path test.
hints: Start by answering the question for one node only, the root. What does a single leaves-upward pass give you, and what does it not?
You are moving an answer along one edge, from a parent to a child. How does the distance to each of the other n-1 nodes change, and how many nodes fall into each case?
The second pass needs the subtree sizes from the first pass, so decide what you store per node before you write either loop.
refs: LC 834 Sum of Distances in Tree
LC 2581 Count Number of Possible Root Nodes

title: A whole binomial row mod p
prompt: Write binomialRow(n int, p int) []int returning C(n,0), C(n,1), ... C(n,n), each reduced mod p. p is prime and larger than n, and n can be 0. The tests go up to n = 1000000, where building Pascal's triangle is about 5*10^11 additions and never finishes, so you need the multiplicative step and therefore division mod p.
explanation: C(n,k) = C(n,k-1) * (n-k+1) / k, so a whole row is one pass if you can divide mod p. You cannot divide, but p is prime and k < p, so k has an inverse and dividing is multiplying by it. Two ways to get the inverses: Fermat gives inv(k) = k^(p-2) mod p in O(log p) each, which is O(n log p) for the row and passes comfortably; the linear table above is the sharper one. It comes from writing p = q*k + r with q = p/k and r = p%k, which mod p says q*k + r = 0, so k^-1 = -q * r^-1, and r < k means the value is already computed. That fills inv[1..n] in O(n) with no exponentiation at all. Two failure modes to keep in mind: doing the division with integer / gives garbage the moment it is not exact, and this whole approach needs p prime and p > n, because otherwise some factor of k! is divisible by p and has no inverse (Lucas' theorem is the fix when p is small).
hints: Do not build the triangle. What is the ratio between two neighbouring entries of one row?
That ratio needs a division by k. Since the modulus is prime, what does that division turn into?
Fermat gives one inverse per call. If you want all of 1..n, look at what p / k and p mod k tell you about k.
refs: LC 1467 Probability of a Two Boxes Having The Same Number of Distinct Balls

title: Convex hull by monotone chain
prompt: Write convexHull(points [][]int) [][]int, each point a []int{x, y}. Return the hull vertices counter-clockwise starting from the lexicographically smallest point (smallest x, then smallest y), dropping duplicates and any point lying on a hull edge rather than at a corner. Fewer than three distinct points, or all of them collinear, returns just the distinct extremes. It must be O(n log n): one test feeds 300001 points that are all hull vertices, where a gift-wrapping march is O(n^2) and takes minutes.
explanation: Andrew's monotone chain: sort by (x, y), then sweep left to right building the lower chain and right to left building the upper chain, popping the previous vertex whenever the last three points do not turn strictly left. Concatenating the two chains with each one's last point dropped gives the closed hull once, counter-clockwise, starting at the lexicographically smallest point, which is why no separate rotation step is needed. The sort dominates at O(n log n) and each point is pushed and popped at most once per chain. The whole geometric content is the cross product (a-o) x (b-o): positive means o->a->b turns left, zero means collinear, negative means right. Popping on <= 0 drops points that sit on an edge; popping on < 0 keeps them, which is the same hull as a shape but a different answer as a list, so decide which one the problem wants. Everything stays in integers, so there is no floating point error to reason about, only overflow: the cross product multiplies coordinate differences, so with coordinates up to 10^9 the intermediate is up to 4*10^18 and only just fits in int64.
hints: Sorting by x first means you are never inserting into the middle of anything. What can you maintain as a stack while sweeping left to right?
Three consecutive points on the chain either turn one way, turn the other, or are flat. Which of those three cases means the middle point cannot be a vertex?
One sweep only gives you half the boundary. What is the cheapest way to get the other half, and where do the two halves overlap?
